deleted.title: Chat
deleted.caption:
Every AI tool I tried died the same way.
I had to paste my whole context in again every single time.

- - -

So I stopped collecting tools and put the work in one place instead. Before that I ran a tab for research, a tab for the CRM, a doc of prompts I kept rewriting and a notes file I pasted from every single morning. Every GTM job I run now opens in the same chat box, the same way, with the same memory sitting underneath it. No new tab to find, no blank screen to fill, no pasting last week's notes back in to remind it who I am. It either already knows, or it asks me once and keeps it. That one change did more for my output than any model upgrade ever did.

- - -

Here is what one chat box actually carries.

→ Five agents behind one slash. I type /specter to research an account, /striker to write the message, /cortex to score the ICP, /pulse to route the model and /sentinel to audit the output. No app switching, no copy paste between them.

→ A tier picker on every turn. Lite for quick lookups, Smart for the real work, Deep when the judgement is hard. I spend on deep thinking only when the turn actually earns it.

→ Memory injected on every turn. Profile, saved facts and open work get stitched into one short block, so I stop re-explaining who I am and what I am building.

→ Attachments it actually reads. PDFs, images, audio, spreadsheets and URLs turn into working context, not a wall of text the model skims and forgets.

→ Sessions that persist and fork. Every chat stays searchable in the sidebar, I can branch one into two without losing the thread, and a read-only link hands the whole thing to someone else.

- - -

The lesson was not that I needed a smarter model. A smarter model on its own changed almost nothing. The model was only ever as good as the context and the tools sitting next to it, and for two years I kept those in a dozen different places. Most founders keep shopping for the model. The leverage was never there. Put them one keystroke apart and the chat box stops being a demo you show people and starts being where the work gets done.

materials.title: Platform Overview
materials.caption:
Your default AI is the wrong tool for most of your GTM. Not because it is weak, because it is one model doing eight different jobs that each break in a different place.

- - -

I spent a quarter running lead research, ICP scoring, cold outreach, call prep, proposals, objection handling, and follow-up through the same AI. The output looked fine and closed nothing. I kept tuning prompts, assuming the prompt was the problem. It was not. Every founder I know is doing the work of a five person GTM team alone, and a smarter model just produces more polished noise faster. The problem was never which model is smartest. It was that I was asking one model to win eight jobs it was never built to win, and a better prompt cannot fix a wrong-model choice.

- - -

So I ran all eight through Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity and kept score. Here is what actually wins:

→ Lead research goes to Perplexity. It pulls live funding and hiring signals before you write a single word, where the others guess.
→ Account enrichment goes to Gemini. Long context, reads Google-native data without truncating halfway through.
→ ICP scoring, cold outreach, call prep, proposals, and objection handling go to Claude. It holds your tone, scores fit honestly, and finds the one issue that quietly loses the deal.
→ Follow-up to close goes to ChatGPT. It pressure-tests the close logic and surfaces the objection you were about to walk past.
→ Run all eight through any single model and it is the right tool for one of them. The other seven ship on the wrong AI.

- - -

The fix was never a smarter model, and it was never a better prompt. It was a routing layer that sends each job to the AI that wins it, remembers the context across all eight so nothing starts from a blank page, and keeps a human at the gate before anything sends. The models are the engine. The routing layer is the system. That is what Ultron runs for you, so you stop deciding which tab to open and start shipping.

- - -

Save this routing map before your next AI subscription.

Follow for one AI system for founders every day.

materials.title: Jobs
materials.caption:
Most AI work dies the second you close the tab. Mine kept running in the background, sourced 200 founders, and pinged me the moment it was done.

- - -

I used to babysit long tasks, watching a spinner so I would not lose the run. Then I moved everything that takes more than a few seconds into a background job. Now I send one prompt, close the tab, and the platform runs the whole thing as a mission while I am in meetings. There is no app to keep open and no thread to hold. It finished on its own, dropped the output where I work, and sent me a notification. It does not matter whether the job takes two minutes or two hours, the pattern is the same and my attention is never the thing holding it up.

- - -

→ One prompt becomes a mission of six child jobs. Research found 200 founders, a skill enriched 124 of them at 18 a minute, a subagent scored each against my ICP and kept the top 80, then a sandbox wrote the list into an editable canvas.

→ Anything slow runs off the live chat: a 200-site scrape, a long workflow that polls and waits, a 9am digest on a schedule. The conversation never blocks while it works.

→ A live donut tracks every job and updates without a refresh, so I am watching real progress instead of guessing. The in-flight step streams its own count as it goes.

→ Every job carries a state and a control I can hit. Cancel it, pause it, retry only the step that broke, or resume from a human gate, without restarting the whole run.

→ Nothing leaves in my name until I approve it. The last step is always the human one, by design.

- - -

The unlock was never a faster model. It was work that no longer needs me watching it. When the long jobs run themselves, your own attention stops being the bottleneck, and a hundred small tasks finally happen in parallel instead of one at a time.

- - -

Follow for one AI system for founders every day.

materials.title: Brain
materials.caption:
Most AI tools forget you the second you close the tab. The agents that actually compound do the opposite, they remember every file, every decision and every contract you ever handed them.

- - -

I stopped briefing Claude at the start of each session and started building its memory instead. Every meeting note, every research result, every signed contract goes into one layer it reads before it answers. It already knows who the prospect is, what the offer costs and how I write, so I never repeat context twice. I do not tag anything or remind it of what we did last week. The right memory just shows up. The whole thing lives in four surfaces on one tab, and each one behaves differently on purpose.

- - -

→ Notes are the only surface I write by hand. They stay editable and shareable, and a pricing note that names the product surfaces on its own the next time I ask about pricing.

→ Memories are written by Claude, not me. After ten messages it summarizes the session, then every five after that, and each memory is read-only and indexed so retrieval can find it weeks later.

→ Files stay uploaded once. I drop the brand guide in, then reference it by description for weeks, encrypted at rest, never re-attached to a single turn.

→ Agreements keep the signed PDF forever. The contract skill files each one against the deal and never overwrites a signed copy, even when I redraft the same contract.

→ Retrieval is hybrid and silent. Before every turn the platform pulls the top matches by meaning, by tag and by recency, then stitches them into the prompt as context I never see in the thread.

- - -

The leverage was never a smarter model. It was a model that stops starting from zero. The model did not change, the amount it remembers did. Memory is what turns a hundred disconnected chats into one operator that understands your business a little better every week, without you managing any of it.

- - -

Comment BRAIN and I will send you the exact Claude memory system we run.
